core: Presentation software builds a deck of slides shown in sequence; leading examples are Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, Apple Keynote, and LibreOffice Impress
The slide is the basic unit; a slide layout is a template arrangement of placeholders that hold titles, body text, tables, charts, pictures, and video
A theme/template is a preset group of colors, fonts, effects, background, and layouts applied across the whole presentation to keep the visual design consistent
You build a slide by adding text, images, and simple charts into the placeholders of a chosen layout

A transition is the effect between slides (one per slide, applied to the whole slide); an animation is an effect on a single element within a slide (entrance, exit, emphasis, motion path), and a slide can carry several
Transitions and animations should be used sparingly so they support rather than distract from the message
Presenter (presenter/presenter-view) mode shows the speaker their notes, the next slide, and controls on their own screen, while the audience sees only the slides

Slide-design best practice is grounded in the limits of working memory: keep slides uncluttered, few words, one idea per slide, large readable fonts, high contrast, and visuals over walls of text, because an audience cannot read dense text and listen at the same time
Finished decks can be presented as a full-screen slideshow and exported to other formats such as PDF
supporting: Placeholders are the dotted-line containers on a layout that pre-format where content goes
Common built-in layouts include a Title slide and a Title and Content slide
Standard editing views include a normal/editing view, an outline view, a notes view, and a slide-sorter view for reordering
Text below roughly 22 point is hard for an audience to read; white-on-dark or black-on-light give safe high contrast
Slides are visual reinforcement of the talk, not the speaker's script or a printed handout
outOfScope: Word processing and document formatting (owned by Word Processing)
Spreadsheet mechanics and chart data modeling (owned by Spreadsheets; presentation software only embeds simple charts)
Real-time co-editing and comments on shared decks (owned by Collaboration Platforms)
Detailed accessibility/contrast standards and alt text (kept to general readability here)
File-format internals of .pptx/.odp/.key (owned by File Extensions)

claims.claim: Presentation software organizes content into a sequence of slides; widely used examples include Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, Apple Keynote, and LibreOffice Impress.

A slide layout is a template that contains the formatting, positioning, and placeholder boxes for a slide's content; placeholders are the dotted-line containers that hold titles, body text, tables, charts, pictures, and video.
Common built-in layouts include a Title slide and a Title and Content slide, and the colors, fonts, effects, and background of a slide are collectively called its theme.

A theme is a preset group of colors, fonts, background, and layouts; applying one theme sets a consistent visual design across the whole presentation, and a layout is the way text and images are arranged on a slide.

Impress lets a user create slides that contain text, bulleted and numbered lists, tables, charts, and graphic objects such as drawings and photographs, along with animation and slide-transition effects, and offers Normal, Outline, Notes, and Slide Sorter views.
A transition is the special effect that occurs when you move from one slide to the next; it applies to an entire slide and only one transition can be applied per slide.

An animation is a special effect applied to a single element on a slide (text, a shape, an image), in four categories - entrance effects make an object appear, exit effects make it disappear, emphasis effects draw attention to a visible object, and motion paths move an object - and one slide can have several animations.
Presenter view lets the speaker see the presentation with speaker notes on their own computer while only the slides appear on the screen the audience sees.

When a slide holds too much text, audience members must choose between reading the text and listening to the speaker because they cannot do both; slides work best as visual reinforcement of the talk rather than as the speaker's script.

Effective presentation aids are direct and uncluttered, use text large enough to read (roughly 22 point or larger) and high contrast between text and background, because novel information must first pass through a working memory that is limited in capacity and duration.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder text with sourced definitions of slides, layouts, placeholders, themes, transitions vs animations, presenter view, and design-for-cognitive-load principles.
Named PowerPoint, Google Slides, Keynote, and Impress only as examples of the software category, per subject caution to describe categories generically.

Grounded the 'few words / visuals over walls of text' advice in the working-memory limits of cognitive load theory and the OER's audience-cannot-read-and-listen point, rather than asserting it as unsourced style opinion.
Handed document formatting to Word Processing, chart/data modeling to Spreadsheets, co-editing to Collaboration Platforms, and file-format internals to File Extensions per anti-duplication guidance.

sourceRecords.title: What is a slide layout?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: slide layouts are templates that contain formatting, positioning, and placeholder boxes for the content on a slide; placeholders are the dotted-line containers that hold titles, body text, tables, charts, SmartArt, pictures, clip art, videos, and sounds; the colors, fonts, effects, and background of a slide are collectively the theme; named examples include the Title slide and Title and Content layout. sourceRecords.title: The difference between animations and transitions
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: an animation is a special effect that applies to a single element on a slide (text, shape, image); a transition is the special effect when you exit one slide and move to the next; a transition applies to an entire slide and only one transition can be applied per slide; the four animation categories are entrance (make an object appear), exit (make it disappear), emphasis (draw attention to a visible object), and motion paths (move an object). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Reference-only; original wording used.

sourceRecords.title: Present on multiple monitors (and view speaker notes privately)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: Presenter view lets you view the presentation with speaker notes on one computer (e.g., your laptop) while only the slides themselves appear on the screen the audience sees; on the Slide Show tab, Use Presenter View enables it, and newer versions set it up automatically when a second monitor is connected. Verified via WebSearch result text quoting the Microsoft Support page on 2026-08-19. Reference-only; original wording used.

sourceRecords.provider: Barton & Tucker, Dalton State College (Maricopa Open Digital Press)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: when a slide has too much text the audience must choose between reading it and listening, and an audience member cannot do both; slides are best used for visual reinforcement and clarification rather than as a script; each aid should be a direct, uncluttered example of a specific point; use text large enough to read (avoid fonts much smaller than 22 point, especially on handouts) and high contrast such as white on dark or black on light backgrounds. sourceRecords.title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later (Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292)
sourceRecords.provider: John Sweller, Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer, Fred Paas; ERIC record EJ1217401
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the source registry. Used for the cognitive-load premise behind slide-design advice: novel information is first processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration before being stored in long-term memory, so overloading a slide with text and effects competes with the listener's limited processing capacity. Abstract-level verification only; no wording reproduced.
